questions.question: What is biotechnology?
choices: Study of biological classification without practical applications
Observation of ecosystems without changing or using biological processes
Study of chemical elements without living systems
Use of organisms or biological processes to make useful products

questions.question: What is a plasmid?
choices: A small DNA molecule separate from a bacterium's main chromosome
A protein that makes up a cell membrane
A sugar stored in plant roots
A structure that carries oxygen in blood

questions.question: What do restriction enzymes do?
choices: Copy every protein in a cell
Cut DNA at particular sequences
Join amino acids into carbohydrates
Sort chromosomes by mass

questions.question: What is the main purpose of PCR?
choices: Sorting DNA fragments by their movement through a gel
Cutting DNA at selected recognition sites
Making many copies of a selected DNA region
Joining fragments of DNA into one molecule

questions.question: What does gel electrophoresis commonly separate?
choices: DNA fragments only by their original organism
Whole chromosomes only by gene function
Cells only by their rate of reproduction
DNA fragments by size

questions.question: What is recombinant DNA?
choices: DNA assembled from different sources
Any DNA without chemical bonds
DNA found only in extinct organisms
A protein made of joined chromosomes

questions.question: What is a genetically modified organism?
choices: Any organism that grows larger than its parent
An organism whose DNA has been deliberately changed using genetic technology
An organism with no genetic material
Any organism produced by ordinary fertilization

questions.question: Why can bacteria be used to produce human insulin?
choices: Bacteria absorb insulin directly from the surrounding air
Bacteria always produce insulin without an inserted gene
An introduced gene can direct production of the insulin protein
Insulin production requires bacteria to develop human organs

questions.question: Why does a PCR procedure need primers?
choices: They cut away the target region before copying
They prevent the target sequence from being copied
They separate fragments according to size after copying
They specify starting points for copying the target region

questions.question: In a DNA gel, why do shorter fragments generally travel farther under the same conditions?
choices: They move more easily through the gel's pores
They carry no electrical charge
They contain more total DNA than longer fragments
They turn into proteins during separation

questions.question: Why are controls important in a DNA detection experiment?
choices: They guarantee every sample contains the target
They help reveal contamination or a failed procedure
They establish an organism's identity without testing DNA
They prevent every mutation during DNA copying

questions.question: How is selective breeding different from direct gene editing?
choices: It changes a chosen DNA sequence directly in every offspring
It requires inserting a new gene with a molecular tool
It chooses parents rather than directly changing a selected DNA sequence
It chooses parents without affecting inherited trait frequencies

questions.question: What does a DNA sequence comparison between two samples directly show?
choices: Complete proof of every trait they express
The exact age of their owners
Whether either sample has never mutated
Similarities and differences in their tested sequences

questions.question: Why does changing a gene not guarantee one simple visible outcome?
choices: Traits may depend on gene interactions and environment
Genes have no effect on proteins
Every trait depends on one gene alone
The environment replaces all DNA

questions.question: What is an important difference between cloning a DNA fragment and cloning an organism?
choices: Both always create a new species
One copies a sequence; the other produces a whole organism
One removes all genes; the other removes all cells
Both require fertilization of an egg by two sperm

questions.question: A DNA gel shows a sample band at the same position as a known 300-base-pair marker. What does this suggest?
choices: The sample has exactly 300 genes
The organism is 300 years old
The fragment is approximately 300 base pairs long
The fragment encodes 300 proteins

questions.question: A negative PCR control containing no sample DNA produces the target band. What should researchers suspect?
choices: Every sample is proven free of contamination
The negative control confirms that the target is absent
The sample bands can be accepted without further checks
Contamination of reagents or the procedure

questions.question: A bacterium receives a gene but produces no detectable protein. Which follow-up addresses a relevant possibility?
choices: Check whether the gene is expressed under the culture conditions
Assume all inserted DNA always produces protein
Measure only the color of the incubator
Conclude that bacteria never make proteins

questions.question: A proposed crop modification reduces insect damage. Which evidence would best assess a possible ecological tradeoff?
choices: Only the yield of plants under one growing condition
Effects on both target pests and nearby non-target organisms
Only whether the inserted sequence can be copied
Only the modified crop's appearance at harvest

questions.question: Two DNA samples match at one tested region. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: They must come from the same individual
They must have identical complete genomes
They match at that region, but more evidence is needed to establish identity
They cannot come from related individuals
